newsitem.title: GERMANY: German economics minister attacks Waigel on tax.
newsitem.headline: German economics minister attacks Waigel on tax.

text.p: Embattled Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Sunday drew a sharp rebuke from a fellow minister for blaming others for the budget woes threatening Germany's bid to qualify for European monetary union (EMU).

Waigel, in an interview with news weekly Der Spiegel, said other government departments had botched economic forecasts and left him searching for billions of marks to cut Bonn's budget deficit to meet EMU's convergence criteria.
But Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt hit back, saying Waigel was "playing the wrong game" and that his remarks were a "transparent manoeuvre to distract from his own faults".

Government feuding broke out into the open after Waigel refused to rule out tax hikes to cut the budget deficit to the limit of three percent of gross domestic product required by the Maastricht treaty to join EMU's starting lineup in 1999.

Waigel has also come under fire over a controversial plan to revise up the value of the Bundesbank's gold and foreign exchange reserves, a move he says would help cut both the national debt and the budget deficit.

Although Waigel cuts a powerful image on the international stage, his domestic influence is constrained since the growth forecasts on which he bases his budget are made by Rexrodt's department and unempoyment outlooks come from the Labour Ministry.
"If (the Economics Minister) gets it wrong...then the Finance Minister has to cope with the consequences," he told Spiegel in an interview from the magazine's Monday edition.
But, in a statement on official ministry paper, Rexrodt retorted: "It is always the Finance Ministry which presses for a more favourable economic forecast."

Unemployment, which peaked in January at a 64-year record of 4.7 million, has blown away Bonn's budget projections. And recent tax projections revealed a new gap of nearly 20 billion marks ($12 billion) in revenues this year.
Rexrodt's Free Democrat party (FDP), junior partners in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition, passed a resolution on Sunday rejecting tax increases to plug the budget holes.
"Anything else would undermine the foundations of this coalition," FDP parliamentary leader Hermann Otto Solms told a party conference in Wiesbaden.
Waigel told Spiegel he could not rule out tax hikes.
"We must exhaust all options to avoid tax increases," he said. "But a finance minister who ruled that out now would be irresponsible."

He also mounted a vigorous defence of his decision to mark up the value of Germany's gold and foreign exchange reserves -- which are valued by the Bundesbank at their historic lows -- up to reflect current market values.
Revaluing the reserves was an "absolutely legitimate and economically clean" move, he told Spiegel, adding it would have a positive impact on meeting the Maastricht criteria.
The idea has outraged Bonn's European partners and led to cries of "fudge" and creative accounting. German commentators have been equally scathing of Waigel.
"Waigel has still not come up with a concrete plan to save the budget," commented news magazine Focus, casting Waigel in the role of the "permanent victim".

Focus said Waigel was a prisoner to the interests of the FDP, hostage to a blockade of tax legislation by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) and threatened by his own party friends from his Bavarian power base.
But the SPD, which has threatened to block in parliament a government package of 30 billion marks ($18 billion) in longer-term tax cuts, was not doing much better at the weekend.

Party leader Oskar Lafontaine announced details of a long-awaited SPD tax reform policy which he said would cut income and corporate taxes and boost child allowances to leave the average worker 2,500 marks ($1,500) a year better off.

The Welt am Sonntag newspaper said some SPD leaders, including Lafontaine's leadership rival Gerhard Schroeder, were still not happy with the tax position. Party leaders meet on Monday to review the policy document. ($ = 1.693 German Marks)
